sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's string model trips up almost every developer coming from Python or Java because Go strings are byte sequences, not character sequences. The rune/byte distinction, the `len()` vs character-count difference, and the lack of implicit type conversion are all fresher interview staples. Getting these right shows you have actually written Go that handles real-world text.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Two distinctions to anchor everything:

- **`byte` is a raw byte (uint8), `rune` is a Unicode character (int32).** `len("café")` returns `5` because `é` is a 2-byte UTF-8 sequence. `len([]rune("café"))` returns `4`. When iterating with `range`, Go gives you runes — the right default for text processing.
- **Go has zero implicit type conversions.** You cannot add an `int` and a `float64` without an explicit cast — `float64(i) + f`. Coming from Python (duck typing) or JavaScript (coercion), this feels strict at first but eliminates a whole class of subtle numeric bugs.
- **`strings.Builder` is the correct tool for building strings in a loop** — like Java's `StringBuilder`. Concatenating with `+` in a loop is O(n²) and should be avoided.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **String immutability** — a Go string is a read-only slice of bytes; you cannot modify `s[0] = 'X'`; to modify, convert to `[]byte` or `[]rune`, mutate, then convert back
- **Rune vs byte** — `byte` = `uint8` = raw byte in memory; `rune` = `int32` = Unicode code point; multi-byte UTF-8 characters have `len > 1` bytes but are a single rune
- **String iteration** — `for i, ch := range s` iterates runes (correct for text); `for i := 0; i < len(s); i++` iterates bytes (useful for ASCII only)
- **strings package** — `strings.Contains`, `strings.HasPrefix`, `strings.Split`, `strings.Join`, `strings.TrimSpace`, `strings.ToLower`, `strings.Builder` for efficient concatenation
- **strconv package** — `strconv.Atoi(s)` string to int; `strconv.Itoa(n)` int to string; `strconv.ParseFloat`, `strconv.FormatFloat`; always returns an error on invalid input
- **Type conversion vs type assertion** — `int(f)` is a type conversion (between numeric types); `v, ok := x.(string)` is a type assertion (interface → concrete type)
- **fmt.Sprintf** — `fmt.Sprintf("%d items at $%.2f each", count, price)` for formatted string building; `%v` for default format, `%T` for type name, `%q` for quoted string

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **`len("café") == 5` not 4** — `é` is encoded as 2 bytes in UTF-8. The correct way to count characters is `len([]rune(s))` or `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)`. Interviewers ask: 'how do you get the character count of a string?'
- **Modifying a string index panics** — `s[0] = 'H'` is a compile error (strings are immutable). To mutate, do `b := []byte(s); b[0] = 'H'; s = string(b)`.
- **`strconv.Atoi` vs `fmt.Sscanf`** — always use `strconv.Atoi` for string-to-int conversion in interviews; it returns an explicit error. `fmt.Sscanf` is for parsing formatted input.
- **Type assertion panics without the ok form** — `v := x.(string)` panics if `x` does not hold a string. The safe form is `v, ok := x.(string); if ok { ... }`. Always use the two-value form in production code.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In Go, strings are immutable byte sequences. `len()` counts bytes, not characters — so for Unicode text I use `range` to iterate runes or convert to `[]rune` first. Go has no implicit numeric type conversion, so I explicitly cast with `int()`, `float64()` and so on. For string-to-number conversion I use the `strconv` package, which returns an error I can check, unlike a silent coercion that could hide bugs."*
